# The Mud-Engine and the Free Pond

Listen close, little wrigglers. Gather round the lily-pad shadow. Old Gristle-Toad has a tale for you.

Back before your eggs were even dreamed, the Great Silt War came to our pond. Not a war of teeth and claws—worse. The Upstream Dam-Folk decided they'd control the water flow. Open the gates when they pleased. Close them when they pleased. We'd choke in mud or drown in flood, depending on their whim.

Now, some creatures would've picked a Chief. Some would've begged the Dam-Folk for mercy. Not us.

We built the Mud-Engine.

Picture this: a great churning beast of woven reeds and river-stones, powered by nothing but the current itself. No single toad owned it. No council voted on when it ran. Every morning, whoever woke up hungry for work would swim to their station. The strong ones turned the main wheel. The clever ones watched the pressure-gauges made of hollow snail shells. The tiny ones—you, someday—would dart through the intake tubes, clearing debris with your small tails.

No one told us what to do. We just... did it. Because the pond was ours, and the Engine kept it breathing.

The Dam-Folk laughed. "Without a King to command you, you'll scatter like minnows!" they croaked through their reed-speakers.

But here's the thing they never understood: we didn't need commands. We had something better.

We had *agreements*.

When Kelp-Toad's hatchlings got sick, three other families moved into her burrow without being asked. When the winter ice cracked the northern intake, twelve toads showed up at dawn with clay and spine-needle thread. Not because they were ordered. Because they saw the problem, and it was *their* problem too.

The Engine ran for seven seasons. Seven seasons of free water, clean mud, and tadpoles who grew up knowing they were capable creatures.

Then came the day the Dam-Folk tried to sabotage us. They sent their otter mercenaries—sleek, paid killers—to jam the main wheel with river-trash.

What they didn't expect: every toad in the pond felt the vibration change. Not through orders. Through the water itself. The Engine hummed differently, and we all heard it.

Within minutes, fifty toads swarmed the intake. We didn't wait for a general. We didn't form ranks. We just became what the moment needed. The big ones held the debris. The fast ones cut it free. The old ones like me directed the flow with croaks and gestures.

The otters fled. Not because we defeated them in battle. Because they couldn't fight something that had no head to cut off.

Afterward, we didn't celebrate a victory. We celebrated each other. We passed around the warm clay-pipes and told stories of who did what. No medals. No promotions. Just knowing: *I am useful. My kin are useful. Together, we are unstoppable.*

That's the secret, little wrigglers. That's what makes our pond different.

We don't wait for permission to care for each other.
We don't need a whip to know when work needs doing.
We don't bow. We build.

The Dam-Folk still have their gates and their guards and their endless meetings about who gets to decide what. Good for them. That's their way.

Our way is simpler: see a need, fill it. See a neighbor, help them. See a problem, solve it together.

You'll grow legs. You'll leave the water. You'll build your own machines—maybe better than the Mud-Engine, maybe stranger. But remember this feeling: the hum of the wheel, the press of your kin against you in the current, the knowledge that no one owns you and you own everything worth owning.

You are tadpoles of the Free Pond. You are already whole. You are already enough.

Now go on. The intake tube needs clearing, and I'm too old for the small passages.

*Old Gristle-Toad settles back into the mud, watching the little tails disappear into the green water. Somewhere, the Engine hums on.*
